generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, honest and balanced reflection matters in every subject, because so much of study can invite self-doubt: a task that felt awkward, a session that went poorly, a result you did not expect. A reflection that is all self-criticism, or all excuses, teaches you little. Looking at what went well as well as what did not, and owning your own part fairly, is what makes reflection genuinely useful, whatever you study.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two students reflect on the same presentation that fell flat.

Student A writes only the negatives: 'I was terrible. I froze, I rushed, the whole thing was a disaster and everyone could tell. I am just not good at this.' This is honest about the difficulty, but it is one-sided and harsh. It names no positives, turns a single session into a verdict on the person, and offers nothing to build on.

Student B reflects on the same session in balance: 'The start was shaky and I rushed when I lost my place. But I had prepared the material well, and the main point I made landed, because two people picked it up afterwards. I froze mainly because I was reading from dense notes. Next time I will use short prompts instead.' This looks at the positives first, is honest about the difficulty without being cruel, and finds something to change.

Both found the session hard. Only Student B reflected in a way that was honest, balanced, and actually useful.
generatedProse.summary: A reflection is only useful when it is honest and balanced: looking at the positives first, never landing all on one side, and being truthful about your own part without being harsh. You can now explain why balance matters, tell a balanced reflection from a one-sided one, and recognise what makes a reflection honest rather than defensive or self-critical. With what reflection is, a simple model, and the honesty to use it well, you are ready to reflect on purpose, in any subject you study.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Student B's reflection more balanced than Student A's?

items.text: It named what went well and what went badly, honestly and without being harsh.
It was more negative about the person's own ability.
It avoided mentioning anything that went wrong.
It was shorter and stuck to the facts.

feedback.correct: That's right. Naming both what went well and what went badly, fairly, makes it balanced.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. A balanced reflection includes both sides; which option does that?
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B's reflection was balanced because it named the good and the bad honestly and fairly. Being more negative, or ignoring the negatives, is one-sided.
